The Backstory, or, Does this Sound Like You?

Hi all, I'm new to the sub and thought I'd share a bit of knowledge that helped me much later than I'd have liked it to.

I was self-taught, and like many eager newbies I wanted to get to shredding as fast as possible. I practiced often, hard, and like a good little boy always with my metronome. But, I did NOT practice right, and after about a year of playing, I could not figure out why I couldn't get past 16ths in the 160-180 range. I had good days where I'd hit 180, and bad days where I couldn't go past 150. After months in this rut I figured I surely should have progressed by now. No dice.

What My Problem Was

Immense tension, total lack of finger independence, terrible posture, and constant practice with these terrible habits were all keeping me stagnant. I took video of my playing and my problem was identified across many online forums almost immediately. Like many, I'd been told that fretting 1-2-3-4-4-3-2-1 all day long was going to get me my speed. Really, all it got me was the ability to roll my wrist and totally ignore finger strength, independence, speed, and a whole lot of tension.** But the exercise didn't dig the hole I had found myself in, my total disregard for relaxation and finger independence did. 1-2-3-4 can work, but only if you're mindful.**

The Symptoms

Sore fingers, wrist, and/or forearm after trying to play fast. Rolling your wrist. Plateauing. The "floating pinky." Inability to fully fret a note. All signs you need work on finger independence.

Fixing The Problem, or For 5 payments of 19.99! (just kidding)

This was the bummer. Bad habit was ingrained in my muscle memory. Just thinking about relaxing wasn't going to cut it. I had to kick the old habit, and make relaxation and finger independence my new habit. This would take time. Lots of it. I knew that going in, and prepared myself. I was directed to a video, and it's a large part of what saved me. A massive part. So here it is, the video that cured me:

Daniel "Freepower" Crawford's Lesson on Finger Independence

note: Crawford is using the pad of his fingers too much in this video. The tips of your fingers are far and away the best spot to contact the string. That being said, don't throw the baby out with the bathwater: this is a great exercise.

Watch the video and live by it until it is your habit. Do what he says. No cheating! That's just a part of it though. I was told, when relaxing between fretting fingers, as Mr. Crawford suggests, to relax my whole body. I was also told to pay very close attention to what my body does when I actually do fret. Am I getting tense anywhere? Am I carrying that tension over into the next fret? I had to be wary of how tense I was getting when I played every note, because I knew the more relaxation I could install into that muscle memory of mine, the more it would pay off in the end.

"Argh, but this is SO FRUSTRATING."

In order to be mindful of this relaxation, you need to go as slow as Crawford suggests. You need that time to check your body for tension. That's what sucks. You know that you're capable of playing much faster, and that thought will creep into your head, and often. You just need to remember, that although you're right, if you go back to your old ways, you'll never kick your habit. You'll never play faster, at least safely, and you have a very high chance of really hurting yourself. After a year of playing how I was, I was already getting some RSI symptoms.

That being said, you need to have some fun.

I needed to remind myself that guitar doesn't need to be all work. I still jammed, and still played what I liked to play, I just tried to keep those bad habits down to a minimum. I made sure to take two steps forward and only one back. The funny thing was, the more I went back to playing how I always had, the more I realized how uncomfortable it was. Which brings me to: ** The Payoff**

It feels SO good to play relaxed, and it's just so much easier. I don't feel limited anymore, and I don't have that weight on me. I since haven't found a single passage or lick or anything that I can't get to by putting the mindful practice in. Yeah, some things take a lot longer, but I see consistent improvement. Those exercises gave me what I needed to move forward. I've still got a lot to learn. A lot. I know I'll never master the guitar, but knowing that I can go as far as I want to is all thanks to this foundation I created with relaxed finger independence.

Spider scales!

The spider scales he refers to involve using different finger patterns, like 2-3-1-4, 4-2-1-3, 4-1-3-2, and so on, also, across different strings, so first note on low e, second on A, etc. The more you do with these patterns, the more strings skipping you do, the different patterns you do, and particularly making up your own will help immensely.

tl;dr: Watch the video in the middle. Live by it, and don't cheat. After putting the time in, enjoy relaxed finger independence.
